# The Devotion deck

**What it rewards:** Belief as a second economy. You earn faith from your land and your practices, spend it where other empires spend production (faith purchases and rites), and spread your religion past your borders. **Directions inside it:** faith purchases and miracles; rites chosen for what they cost and what they give; missionary spread and foreign followers; holy sites and sacred places; holy war; religious learning.

*Initially generated by `scripts/deckDocs.mjs`; now a hand-edited design spec (deck-list pass, 2026-10-06). **Built** means the card exists in the game as written. **Revised** means the card exists (live or as a deferred row) and this sheet changes it; the last column says what changed. **New** means a card proposed by this sheet; the last column says whether existing effect shapes can express it or what new mechanic it needs. **Deferred** means the card is in the data but not built. Government tiers here are proposed availability, not confirmation of runtime unlocks. The generator runs only on request and overwrites these edits.*

**Review (2026-10-06).** Target: about 45 to 55 cards exclusive to the deck. This review took the sheet from 57 to 44: fourteen cuts, one new card (The Offered Stones, the missing Tier III step of the faith-purchase arc), and several cards trimmed to a single job. Three cards moved down to Tier I so the faith-purchase arc opens early. The Quiet Hours is renamed The Octave; The Feast Days is cut (if it returns, it should be called The Jubilee). The reconciliation of the six sheets (2026-10-06) then cut The Endowed Trusts (Commerce's The Waqf keeps the idea), made The Rising Nave a card shared with Magisterial, and cut the shared Harvest Offerings, leaving 42 exclusive cards. The balance pass (2026-10-06) made The Holy Army a card shared with Dominion, cut The Relic Bearers and The Jizya in favour of Dominion's twins (The Oriflamme and Convert It or Tax It, now shared), added The Hymn Schools and the shared The Flood Festival, moved The Priest-Astronomers and The Rites Commonwealth up to Tier I and Consecrated Labor down to Tier 0, and changed several prices. That leaves 40 exclusive cards (7 / 13 / 12 / 5 / 3) and 16 shared ones. The deck's arcs:
- **Faith instead of production.** Workers, tiles and science buildings bought with faith at Tier I (Consecrated Labor, Consecrated Ground, The Monastic Builders), faith given to a build and every building bought with faith at Tier II (The Votive Gifts, The Lay Brothers), buildings bought with faith paying culture at Tier III (The Offered Stones), and at Tier IV faith paid into the Magnum Opus (The Last Offering) and a wonder finished with faith (The Pious Masons). Since the user pass (2026-10-12) the arc has no Tier 0 card.
- **Spreading the faith.** The Calling at Tier 0, The Living Hymnal, The Mission and The Alms Roads at Tier I, Mission Houses at Tier II, The Holy Inquisition at Tier III, The Great Consecration, The Great Commission, The Tithe of Nations, The Conversion of Kings and The Interdict at Tier IV.
- **Holy sites and rites at home.** First Rites and The Holy Spring at Tier 0, The Rites Commonwealth and The Fast at Tier I; holy-site cards at Tier II (The Saints' Fields, The Old Holy Places, Temple Estates); The Monastic University, the shared The Holy Army and The Doctors of the Church at Tier III; The Seven Pilgrimages, The Chapter Houses and The Apostolic Succession at Tier IV.
- Holy war stays an optional strand (The Spiritual Host, The Last Crusade and The Host Restored at Tier IV, and the shared The Oriflamme, Convert It or Tax It and The Holy Army), opened by the shared The Sacred Host and Rites of Passage.

**Tier 0 and Tier IV pass (2026-10-07):** added 3 Tier 0 and 12 Tier IV cards. Tier 0 gains an opener for the spreading arc (The Calling), a first way to put faith into buildings (The Votive Gifts) and a settling choice for sacred places (The Holy Spring). Tier IV now reads: finishers The Great Consecration, The Last Offering and The Tithe of Nations (only the first two touch Opus production); late engines The Treasury of Merit, The Apostolic Succession, The Chapter Houses and The Seven Pilgrimages; pressure The Interdict, The Peace of God and The Last Crusade; big moments The Great Commission, The Year of Grace and The Conversion of Kings; and the deck's signature at its largest in The Pious Masons (faith finishes a wonder) and The Host Restored (a miracle that heals the whole army). New faith prices are written against the faith rate, so they move with the pending ruling on what faith is worth.

**User pass (2026-10-12):** cut The Healing, The Loaves, Sainthood, The Cathedral Fund, The Copying Houses and The Year of Grace. Added The Wayside Shrines (Tier 0), The Painted Chapels (Tier I), The Penitents' Roll (Tier II) and The Learned Clergy (Tier III). Moved Consecrated Labor and The Hymn Schools to Tier I, The Votive Gifts to Tier II and The Creed to Tier I (buffed to +2 and +2 per belief). Revised The Living Hymnal (every following city, no cap) and The Saints' Fields (+5 gold in place of production); The Consolation is no longer a miracle. Smaller wording or number changes on First Rites, Lay Offerings, Temple Estates, The Offered Stones, The Doctors of the Church and The Treasury of Merit. Shared: The Blessed Forges added with Scientific at Tier II; Rites of Passage and The Monastery Libraries kept; The Sacred Host loses its upkeep clause. 55 → 53 exclusive cards; 16 → 17 shared. The Hymn Schools was then removed as a duplicate of The Painted Chapels.

**The production gap.** Devotion is weak at production on purpose. Its answer is faith: buying units, workers, buildings and tiles with faith, and spending faith on rites. Cards that spend faith on an effect (The Host Restored, The Votive Gifts, The Interdict) are built as rites the card unlocks, which reuse the city's rite action (the user, 2026-10-12: a miracle is a rite). Flat production in rite-keeping cities is the pattern the spec tells this deck to avoid, so the first pass cut or revised the cards that did it.

Before the first pass: 44 cards (18 built, 26 deferred). The first pass cut ten and added more, reaching 57. This review cut fourteen and added one, for 44, and the reconciliation took two more off, for 42. The balance pass moved one card to the shared shelf, cut two and added one, for 40. The Tier 0 and Tier IV pass added three and twelve, for 55. The user pass (2026-10-12) cut six and added four, for 53, and added one shared card. With 53 own cards and 17 shared, the shelf is deep enough for eleven chairs: Tiers I and II carry the middle game (fifteen and eleven own cards), Tier 0 has eight own cards (with the shared Sacred Groves and Rites of Passage beside them), Tier III is still thin (five own cards, with the shared The Holy Army and The Rising Nave beside them), and Tier IV has fourteen, enough to fill the late chairs with endgame cards.

| **First Rites** | common | built | +25% production toward Shrines. Shrines give +2 faith. | +25% production toward Shrines · +2 faith in every city with a Shrine. User, 2026-10-12: reworded only (was: "Shrines cost 25% less production and give +2 faith."); the effect is the same |
| **Pastoral Shrines** | common | revised | Worked pastures gain +1 faith and +1 food. A city working at least two pastures gains +1 happiness. | Was (deferred): "...Your capital gains +2 production while you control an improved pasture." The capital-production half was the blocker and also flat production; it is replaced with happiness from herds. Fits existing effects (a hex line on pastures and a "working at least two" city test). |
| **Lay Offerings** | common | revised | Camps and plantations gain +1 faith and +1 food. | Was: "Worked mines and camps gain +1 faith. A city working at least two gains +3 gold, once per city." Mines belong to four other decks, so plantations replace them (Devotion's own family: incense, wine and the other crops of ritual). The review drops the gold clause: gold on plantations is Commerce's side of that shared improvement. Kept as one of the deck's few Tier 0 filler cards, the only one that pays on camps and plantations. Fits existing effects. User, 2026-10-12: adds +1 food and drops "worked" (was: "Worked camps and plantations gain +1 faith."). |
| **The Old Gods Remain** | uncommon | new | Gain one more pantheon belief. | Fits existing effects: the pantheon-slot effect two buildings already use. Beliefs amplified, at the tier where the pantheon is the only belief there is. |
| **The Founding Vows** | uncommon | new | Commission. Start a rite in two different cities while this is seated. Reward: 100 faith, and each of those cities gains one citizen. Then this card leaves its chair. | Needs: commissions. Asks for more rites than the deck would start without it, and is the deck's only early commission. Was: "Commission: have three of your cities keeping a rite at the same time. Reward: 150 faith, and each of those three cities gains +1 population." Balance pass: three rites at once is out of reach for most of Tier 0, so the card sat in one of three chairs doing nothing. |
| **The Calling** | common | new | Prophets cost 30% less faith until you have founded a religion. | Needs: a test for "has not founded a religion yet" (the founding refusals already ask it) and a discount on the prophet's faith price, the shape The Holy Inquisition asks for inquisitors. The spreading arc's opener, which had none at Tier 0: the world holds only so many religions, so the card sets an early race to found one. Stops paying once it has done its job. |
| **The Holy Spring** | common | new | Cities whose centre stands beside a mountain or a lake gain +2 faith and +1 culture. | Needs: a city test for a mountain or lake beside the centre (the inland twin of the coastal test cards already use). The sacred-places opener: it gives the first settlers a reason to choose their spot, and it pays culture, the deck's weak early essential. |
| **The Wayside Shrines** | common | new | Cities with a Shrine gain +2 food and +1 happiness. | Added by the user (2026-10-12). Fits existing effects: a city line in every city with a Shrine, the same test First Rites uses. |

|---|---|---|---|---|
| **The Consolation** | common | new | Cities keeping a rite gain +3 happiness. | Fits existing effects: the keeping-a-rite city test (The Festival Calendar). User, 2026-10-12: no longer a miracle. Takes over The Omen Schools' job as the deck's first science, but pays for keeping a calendar of rites across the empire instead of a flat bonus in each rite city. From the Devotion · Scientific history line (Maya and Babylonian priest-astronomers). Was: Tier 0. Balance pass: moved to Tier I, because it pays nothing until the seat keeps rites. |
| **Consecrated Labor** | common | revised | Cities with a Shrine may buy workers with faith. | Was (deferred, Tier I rare): "Workers may be purchased with faith in Temple cities at their normal equivalent purchase price. Not built: the faith bank sells clergy and houses of learning, and nothing opens it to workers. Balance pass: moved to Tier 0 as a common, needing only a Shrine and without the extra charge, so Devotion has a way to spend faith in its first twenty turns; before this every spending card waited for Tier I. | **The Octave** | uncommon | revised | Rites you start while this is seated last 50% longer. | Was "The Quiet Hours" (deferred): "Rites granted while this is seated last five turns longer." Renamed because a follower belief is already called The Quiet Hours; an octave is the eight days a church festival is extended by. Every rite runs ten turns, so 50% is the same five turns, and written as a share it fits the existing rite-length effect, which removes the blocker. |
| **The Fast** | uncommon | new | Once drafted, unlock the Rite of Fasting. A city keeping it does not grow for ten turns and gains faith equal to its population each turn. A fasting city cannot gain citizens by any means. No chair required. | Needs: a rite row with a cost. Every rite today is a pure blessing; this is the first rite that asks the city to give something up, which is what the spec means by rites as decisions. The deck's only charter, and the row Scientific's early-access cards can reach. Balance pass: without the added sentence, The Loaves (faith for a citizen) could grow a town that is collecting faith for not growing. |
| **The Living Hymnal** | uncommon | revised | Your capital gains +2 science and +2 culture for every city following your religion, with no cap. | Live today: +2 science and +2 culture in your capital per foreign city you were the first to convert (at most +24 of each). User, 2026-10-12: counts every city following your religion and drops the cap. As written it counts your own cities too, which for a Devotion seat is most of the empire. Needs: a count of every city following your religion (the live count reads only foreign cities you converted first). The deck's one card that pays for followers before Tier IV; The Congregation Rolls did the same job and is cut. |
| **The Alms Roads** | uncommon | revised | Your trade routes from Temple cities gain +3 faith. | Was (deferred): "Domestic routes from Temple cities give their destination +3 food and +2 gold. The review dropped the gold, which is Commerce's currency and which Pilgrim Markets already pays on routes. Balance pass: the second sentence ("Foreign ones also press your religion at their destination 10 harder") is dropped. It overlapped Commerce's The Silk Road Monks, which carries religion on routes, and "10 harder" could not be read. Fits existing effects now: a route line narrowed to routes from Temple cities. |
| **The Mission** | uncommon | new | Commission: convert two foreign cities to your religion while this is seated. Reward: a free Apostle in your holy city and 100 culture. | Needs: commissions, and a count of conversions made while the card is seated. Was: "be the first empire to convert two foreign cities". Balance pass: "be the first empire" read as a race the seat could lose, which would leave the card dead in its chair. |
| **Consecrated Ground** | uncommon | revised | You may buy tiles with faith, at half their gold price. | Was (deferred, Tier II): "Purchase legal city tiles with faith instead of gold at the same quoted price. ## Synergies with other decks

### Dominion — the holy war
- **Devotion gives Dominion** faith that supplies the army (faith-bought soldiers through The Sacred Host) and heals it late (The Host Restored), strength inside following territory (The Spiritual Host), and targets: cities that follow your religion are where your army fights best.
- **Dominion gives Devotion** spread by conquest (The Crusader Orders presses your religion into a captured city), captured cities to convert or tax (the shared Convert It or Tax It), and kills that pay faith (The Sacred Host, Rites of Passage).
- **Hooks this sheet creates:** cities following your religion (every spread card), clergy in the field beside the army (the shared The Oriflamme), holy sites for a citadel to stand beside (the shared The Holy Army). **Hooks it reads from Dominion:** captured cities (the shared Convert It or Tax It), kills and units trained (The Sacred Host, Rites of Passage), citadels (the shared The Holy Army).
- **Shared improvements:** camps and pastures, including horses, camels and ivory. Devotion pays faith on them (Pastoral Shrines, Lay Offerings); Dominion counts them for its army.
- **Cards on this sheet that serve the pair:** The Spiritual Host, The Last Crusade (strength against a rival building the Opus, in converted land), The Host Restored (the whole army healed with faith); shared: The Oriflamme, Convert It or Tax It, The Holy Army, The Sacred Host, The Crusader Orders, Rites of Passage.

### Expansionist — sacred land
- **Devotion gives Expansionist** happiness from rites (The Consolation, The Rites Commonwealth) and faith-bought workers (Consecrated Labor).
- **Expansionist gives Devotion** wild land and herds that pay faith, and large cities that hold more followers.
- **Hooks this sheet creates:** faith and happiness; holy sites that raise the hexes around them (Temple Estates). **Hooks it reads from Expansionist:** wild land (Sacred Groves pays on unimproved forest, and tended land is still wild), burning seasons (the shared The Flood Festival), pastures (Pastoral Shrines), population (The Fast).
- **Shared improvements:** none on the family lists. The pair meets on wild land; pastures are the fallback overlap, and Pastoral Shrines pays faith on them.
- **Cards on this sheet that serve the pair:** Temple Estates, Pastoral Shrines, Consecrated Labor; shared: Sacred Groves, The Flood Festival.
- **Not carded:** the flood festival is now the shared The Flood Festival, a one-off faith payout when a town starts a burning season rather than a rite-gated flat card. Monks who tend or claim land would need a new religious-unit action; songlines (holy sites joined by road) were cut because they needed a road count no other card uses. All stay ideas for now.

### Commerce — pilgrims and markets
- **Devotion gives Commerce** pilgrims: holy sites as route destinations that pay faith and gold (Pilgrim Markets), and faith turned into gold (The Tithe).
- **Commerce gives Devotion** trade routes that pay faith (The Alms Roads) and carry religion (Commerce's The Silk Road Monks), and gold turned into faith (Commerce's The Waqf).
- **Hooks this sheet creates:** holy sites and follower cities at the end of a route. **Hooks it reads from Commerce:** trade routes, and the record of which bank paid for a building (The Offered Stones reads it for faith, as The Endowment reads it for gold).
- **Shared improvements:** plantations (incense, wine, silk). Devotion pays faith on them (Lay Offerings); Commerce pays gold.
- **Gap covered:** none, deliberately. Both are weak at production; the pair buys everything twice over, with gold and with faith (The Lay Brothers beside Commerce's purchases). This is the first pair to check in playtesting.
- **Cards on this sheet that serve the pair:** The Alms Roads, The Offered Stones, Lay Offerings, The Saints' Fields (gold on Holy Sites since the user pass); shared: Pilgrim Markets, The Tithe.

### Scientific — scholars of the faith
- **Devotion gives Scientific** religious learning (Cloister Schools, The Cloister), faith that buys science buildings (The Monastic Builders), and science from the faith the empire makes (The Learned Clergy).
- **Scientific gives Devotion** religious unlocks ahead of their age. Devotion's charter (The Fast) is the row Scientific's early-access cards can reach.
- **Hooks this sheet creates:** faith, and holy sites for academies to stand beside (The Monastic University). **Hooks it reads from Scientific:** academies, libraries and universities, and unlocks that arrive early.
- **Shared improvements:** plantations (faith for Devotion, science for Scientific), holy sites beside academies, and improved strategic resources (the shared The Blessed Forges).
- **Cards on this sheet that serve the pair:** The Priest-Astronomers, The Monastic Builders, The Monastic University, The Living Hymnal (science from following cities), The Treasury of Merit (science from the faith bank), The Learned Clergy (science from faith income), The Penitents' Roll; shared: Cloister Schools, The Cloister, The Monastery Libraries (kept by the user, 2026-10-12), The Blessed Forges. This was the weakest pair; it now has four new cards of its own.

### Magisterial — the cathedral
- **Devotion gives Magisterial** faith that pays for great people and wonders (Sacred Patronage, Sacred Commissions), and holy sites for its any-family work cards.
- **Magisterial gives Devotion** wonders and culture, and boons on draft that can include faith.
- **Hooks this sheet creates:** faith, holy sites (The Old Holy Places, The Saints' Fields), and cathedrals and wonders that pay while they are being built (the shared The Rising Nave). **Hooks it reads from Magisterial:** wonders completed (Sacred Commissions), wonders in progress (The Rising Nave).
- **Shared improvements:** holy sites and landmarks.
- **Cards on this sheet that serve the pair:** The Old Holy Places, The Pious Masons (a half-built wonder finished with faith in a Cathedral city); shared: The Rising Nave, Sacred Commissions, Sacred Patronage.
- **Not carded here:** relics counting as great works. Sainthood, which made relics, was cut by the user (2026-10-12) until relics get more work; whether a relic counts toward Magisterial's work cards is better ruled on that sheet.
